steps.explanationAfterStep: Water is a weak nucleophile, but a carbocation is a very strong electrophile. Oxygen now shares one of its pairs and has three bonds, so it carries the positive charge.
The oxonium ion is a strong acid, about as strong as H₃O⁺, and water is everywhere. After the proton transfer the positive charge sits on the new H₃O⁺.

title: Water and the tert-butyl cation
subtitle: Water adds to the cation, then a second water takes a proton
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 5 (Organic reactions)

oxonium.caption: tert-butyloxonium ion
hintTiers: Which hydrogens are acidic now? Look for the positively charged atom.
A second water takes one of the hydrogens on the positive oxygen. A proton transfer always needs two arrows.
Arrow 1: a lone pair of the free water to a hydrogen on the positive oxygen. Arrow 2: that O–H bond onto the positive oxygen, which becomes neutral.
oxonium.learnerPrompt: The oxygen now has three bonds and a positive charge. Use a second water molecule to make it neutral.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Chloride is a far weaker base than water (HCl is a strong acid), so the proton ends up on water, as H₃O⁺.
The bond breaks towards the more electronegative atom. Hydrogen leaves as H⁺, with no electrons; the bonding pair stays on the other atom.
Losing water just goes back to the cation you started from. Remove a proton instead.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good start: the lone pair makes a new bond to the hydrogen. But that hydrogen now has two bonds, four electrons, and it can hold only two. Which bond must break, and where do its electrons go?

reactants.caption: tert-butyl cation in water, with its chloride counter-ion
hintTiers: Which atom of water has electrons to give, and which carbon is short of electrons?
An oxygen lone pair forms a new bond to the positive carbon. Nothing has to break. One arrow.
One arrow: a lone pair of a water oxygen to the positively charged central carbon.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Water is the solvent. Draw its attack on the tert-butyl cation.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Chloride can attack too: that gives tert-butyl chloride, which simply ionises again in water. Water is the solvent, present in huge excess, so here it is the nucleophile.
That methyl carbon already has four bonds, so it cannot take a fifth. Attack the carbon carrying the positive charge.

mechanismSummary: A lone pair of water attacks the positive carbon of the tert-butyl cation, giving an oxonium ion with three bonds to oxygen. A second water molecule then removes a proton from that oxygen: tert-butanol and H₃O⁺ form.
